summary: Specifies the syntax of text messages sent between computer users as email, including the headers such as From and Date and the message body. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5322.

eli5.summary: An email is like a letter with an envelope. This says how to write the address, date and subject at the top so every mail program can read them.

questions: what does an email message look like

subtitle: The rules for what an email message looks like: header lines, a blank line, then the body.

tldr.problem: Mail systems exchange messages made of text, and every program needs to agree on how the header fields (such as sender, date and subject) and the body are laid out.
tldr.mechanism: A message is lines of US-ASCII text ending in CRLF: header fields written as a name, a colon and a body, then an empty line, then the body. Formal ABNF grammars define each field.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2822 replaced RFC 822 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5322, which is where the current definition of the format lives.

today: RFC 2822 is obsoleted by RFC 5322 and was updated by RFC 5335 and RFC 5336. It obsoleted RFC 822. It was a Proposed Standard.

sections.title: Scope: Content, Not Envelope
sections.content:
RFC 2822 specifies a syntax for text messages sent between computer users as electronic mail. It supersedes RFC 822, updating it to reflect current practice and folding in incremental changes made by other RFCs.

The RFC views a message as an envelope plus contents. The envelope carries whatever is needed to transmit and deliver the message, and is discussed in RFC 2821. This standard covers only the contents. It also gives text messages only: images, audio and other structured data are left to extensions such as the MIME series (RFC 2045 and its companions).

It does not dictate how sites store messages internally, what features a mail system must have, or how user interface programs behave. It does not pick a character encoding for the wire or the disk either.
sections.eli5: This document is only about the letter inside the envelope, not about how the post office carries it. It also only covers plain text, not pictures or sounds.

sections.title: Lines, Header Fields and Body
sections.content:
A conformant message is made of characters with values 1 through 127, read as US-ASCII. It is split into lines, each ended by a carriage return followed by a line feed (CRLF). A message is a header (a run of header fields) followed, optionally, by a body. An empty line separates them.

Each line MUST be no more than 998 characters and SHOULD be no more than 78 characters, not counting the CRLF. The 998 limit exists because many implementations cannot handle longer lines. The 78 recommendation helps displays that would truncate or badly wrap long lines. Receivers should still cope with longer lines for robustness. In the body, CR and LF MUST appear only together as CRLF.

A header field is a field name, a colon, a field body and CRLF. Field names use printable US-ASCII except the colon. Some field bodies are unstructured (any text except CR and LF); others are structured, built from lexical tokens defined in the grammar.

To fit the line limits, a field body can be folded by inserting a CRLF before any white space where the grammar allows folding white space. Unfolding removes any CRLF that is immediately followed by white space, and every field is interpreted in its unfolded form. Folding SHOULD happen at higher-level breaks, for example after a comma in a list. Structured fields may also contain comments in parentheses, which may nest.
sections.eli5: A message is a list of labelled lines at the top, then a blank line, then the note. If a line gets too long you can break it and start the next piece with a space, like wrapping text at the end of a page.

sections.title: Addresses and Mailboxes
sections.content:
An address is either a mailbox or a group. A mailbox normally has an optional display name and an addr-spec in angle brackets, for example a name followed by <jdoe@machine.example>. A bare addr-spec without the name or brackets is also allowed.

An addr-spec is a locally interpreted string, an at-sign, and a domain. The local part is a dot-atom or a quoted string, and when it can be written as a dot-atom that form SHOULD be used. The domain is a dot-atom (a host or mail exchanger name) or a bracketed domain literal holding the host's literal Internet address. How mail is then moved to that host is left to RFC 2821.

Legacy software sometimes puts the person's name in a parenthesised comment after a bare address. Because the meaning of comments is unspecified, implementations SHOULD use the full name and angle-bracket form instead, and SHOULD NOT put comments in address fields.

A group is a display name, a colon, a possibly empty comma-separated list of mailboxes, and a semicolon. It names a set of recipients, and because the list may be empty it can tell readers that a message went to a named set without listing the individual addresses.
sections.eli5: An address is a name tag plus a mailbox location, like Mary at her street. A group is a team name that holds several people, and the team can even be listed without naming everyone on it.

sections.title: The Standard Header Fields
sections.content:
The only required header fields are the origination date and the originator address fields. Everything else is syntactically optional. Fields may appear in any order and are sometimes reordered in transit, but they SHOULD NOT be reordered, and trace and resent fields MUST NOT be reordered.

  • Date holds the date and time the creator considered the message complete and ready to enter the mail system. It uses a day, month name, year of four or more digits, a time and a zone such as -0600. The form +0000 SHOULD be used for UTC, while -0000 means the time has no information about the local zone.
  • From lists the author mailboxes. If it has more than one mailbox, a Sender field naming a single mailbox MUST also appear. Reply-To optionally suggests where replies go; without it, replies SHOULD go to the From mailboxes.
  • To, Cc and Bcc list the primary recipients, the copied recipients and the blind-copied recipients. How Bcc is handled is implementation dependent.
  • Message-ID is a globally unique identifier that every message SHOULD have. In-Reply-To and References hold the identifiers of earlier messages so that replies can be tied into a conversation thread.
  • Subject, Comments and Keywords are human-readable informational fields. A reply MAY begin its subject with Re: , used only once.
  • Resent- fields are added when a user reintroduces a message into the mail system, and Return-Path and Received are trace fields added in transit. Each new set is prepended, so the newest comes first.

Fields not defined in the RFC may be added as optional fields. They MUST NOT reuse a name defined here, and the standard treats them as uninterpreted.
sections.eli5: The top of an email is like the front of a parcel: who it is from, who it is for, the date, and a subject line. Only the date and the sender are truly required. The rest is extra labels you can add.

sections.title: Obsolete Syntax and Changes From RFC 822
sections.content:
Section 4 describes an obsolete syntax: forms from earlier versions or widely used in real messages. The rule is asymmetric. Creators of messages MUST NOT generate these forms, but parsers MUST still accept and interpret them. Taking the section 3 grammar and adding section 4 gives the grammar for reading messages.

The RFC also says that real messages will not always follow even this extended grammar, and that this is no excuse for programs to crash or lose data. Its example is that although lines must be at most 998 characters, silently dropping the excess is not acceptable.

Appendix B lists 31 changes from RFC 822. Examples include allowing four or more digits for the year, making header field order explicit, giving meaning to the -0000 time zone, removing two-digit years and non-numeric time zones from generation, and specifying line length limits and clearer Bcc behaviour.
sections.eli5: Old ways of writing things are like old slang. A new mail program must understand the old slang when reading, but should never use it when writing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC raises three concerns. First, terminal escape sequences: powerful terminals can act on control characters in ways that remap the keyboard, trigger answerback messages that cause commands to be issued on the recipient's behalf, or affect attached devices. Viewers may wish to strip dangerous sequences, but not indiscriminately, because some escape sequences have legitimate uses.

Second, non-text objects in messages raise further issues, discussed in the MIME documents.

Third, Bcc. Mishandling it can reveal confidential information, even the existence of an address. If the Bcc line is removed, a blind recipient has no explicit sign of being blind-copied and could reply to all and accidentally expose that. Implementations need to be careful when processing replies so as not to reveal blind recipients.
sections.eli5: Be careful with secret copies: if someone who was secretly copied hits reply-all, everyone learns they were in on it. Also, strange hidden characters in a message can trick some old terminals.

data.title: Message from one person to another
data.code:
From: John Doe <jdoe@machine.example>
To: Mary Smith <mary@example.net>
Subject: Saying Hello
Date: Fri, 21 Nov 1997 09:55:06 -0600
Message-ID: <1234@local.machine.example>

This is a message just to say hello.
So, "Hello".
